paras: The attempted lynching of William Fiqua took place in downtown Chicago on the night of August 16, 1900, when a crowd chased a Black man accused of snatching a woman's pocketbook and tried to hang him. Police kept hold of him and brought him to the central station beaten but alive. Coming days after anti-Black riots in New Orleans and New York, the incident was reported nationally as a sign that the violence was spreading north.

According to the dispatches, Fiqua (printed also as Fikua, Flqua and Figua) told police he had arrived from Nashville, Tennessee, two days earlier. One account added that police suspected him of shooting Fireman Thomas J. Honore a few days before.

The accounts say he grabbed a pocketbook from a woman at Wabash Avenue and Madison Street and ran west. When Patrolman Stine tried to stop him, he was said to have fired a revolver, and Stine fired back. In the police and wire versions he kept firing as he fled through the downtown streets, putting a bullet through a Pinkerton watchman's cap and clubbing a cabman, John E. Mahar, with the revolver butt. Theater-goers, pedestrians and hotel guests joined the pursuit, and one of them carried a rope.

Exhausted, Fiqua went down under a cab horse, where Policemen Brennan, Sullivan and Dennehy seized him. As officers walked him toward the central station, the crowd shouted "Hang him!" and "Lynch him!", and the Washington Times quoted the cry "Kill the black devil!" Fists struck his head and face, a man threw a noose cut from an awning rope over his head, and another felled him with a loaded cane. The Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski wrote that he would have hung from a lamppost had police not taken the rope off his neck.

At Madison and Clark streets the crowd blocked the officers and, the AP reported, made "a desperate effort" to take him. Police used their clubs, a riot call was sent in, and a patrol wagon carried him the last block to the station. He was reported bruised and beaten about the head and shoulders, with injuries described as not serious.
No report of charges, a hearing or a sentence for Fiqua appears in the coverage, and no one in the crowd is reported arrested.

The Associated Press story ran on August 17 in papers across the country, often on the front page under headlines such as "SPREADS TO CHICAGO," "AND IN CHICAGO, TOO" and "ATTEMPTED LYNCHING." A separate Chicago special, printed in the Washington Times and in short form by the Akron Daily Democrat, opened by saying the city "came near witnessing a repetition of the New Orleans and New York anti-negro riots" and called Fiqua "a negro desperado."

The Saint Paul Globe blamed "unreasoning race hatred" and said the crowd wanted "immediate vengeance on the spot," while still calling Fiqua "a miserable negro pickpocket." The Willmar Tribune said that with mobs in New York and Chicago the North should not "talk very loudly" about the South. Southern writers turned it against Northern critics: the Atlanta Constitution called it "a general beating of colored people," the Houston Post wrote of "a yelling crowd of whites," and Mrs. W. H. Felton and the Georgia Baptist cited it as proof of Northern race prejudice.

The Black weeklies that noticed the incident printed no news report of the incident and mentioned it only in editorials. The American Citizen wrote on August 17 that "Hell has broke loose among and against the negroes. First in New Orleans then in New York, and lastly in Chicago." A week later the Afro-American Advance counted "the attempted lynching of a colored man in Chicago" in an "epidemic of Negrophobia" spreading north, and faulted the president for not speaking out.

The size of the crowd was given as 500 by the AP, 1,000 in a condensed telegram, "thousands" in the Marshalltown dispatch, and 2,000 rising to 3,000 in the Chicago special; the place of his capture also differs from account to account. Most papers date the attack to Thursday night, though the Bossier Banner's news note put it on Wednesday.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Fiqua
bases: A crowd chased a Black man accused of purse-snatching, shouted 'Hang him' and 'Lynch him', put a rope or noose on him and tried to take him from police; he was not killed (A2, A5, A19, A7).

The crowd, numbered from 500 to 3,000, tried without authority to hang him for an alleged theft and shooting, but police kept him and he survived with head injuries described as not serious (A2, A19); this was an attempted lynching, not a killing.

The AP wire (A2), a separate Chicago special (A19), the Marshalltown dispatch (A5) and the local Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski (A6, A7) agree on the theft accusation, the chase, the rope and the crowd's failed attempt to take him from police.

accounts.label: AP wire
accounts.gist: Fikua snatched a pocketbook, fired three times during the chase, was caught under a horse at the Great Northern Hotel; a crowd of 500 with ropes tried to take him at Madison and Clark until police clubs got him into the patrol wagon.

accounts.label: Chicago special dispatch
accounts.gist: A crowd of 2,000 to 3,000 chased 'a negro desperado' who fired repeatedly; once caught he was beaten, noosed with an awning rope and struck with a loaded cane before a riot call brought the wagon.

accounts.label: Chicago Polish daily
accounts.gist: Will Fikua fired at Officer Brennan, fell under cab wheels, and had a rope put round his neck; he would have hung from a lamppost had police not removed it.

accounts.label: Black editorials
accounts.gist: The Chicago attempt was the latest of a run of anti-Black outbreaks in New Orleans and New York.

framing.detail: The AP story ran under headlines such as 'SPREADS TO CHICAGO', 'AND IN CHICAGO, TOO' and 'ATTEMPTED LYNCHING', calling him a man who 'came dangerously near being lynched'.
The Chicago special called him 'a negro desperado' who 'ran amuck' while reporting the crowd's cry 'Kill the black devil!'.
The Saint Paul Globe condemned the mob's 'immediate vengeance' while calling him 'a miserable negro pickpocket'.
Southern papers (Atlanta Constitution, Houston Post, Mrs. Felton, Georgia Baptist) used the Chicago crowd to rebuke Northern criticism of the South or argue for separation.
The Afro-American Advance called it part of an 'epidemic of Negrophobia' 'born of a malignant hatred for the black man'.

conflicts.note: No account is clearly better; all are unsourced wire figures.
